newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Don't read too much into Taiwan stock surge - Chiang.
newsitem.headline: Don't read too much into Taiwan stock surge - Chiang.

text.p: Taiwan's top economic planner on Thursday said some shares may have been bid up by speculators and that the stock index's surge through 10,000 does not necessarily reflect the island's economic strength.

"The index standing above 10,000 can be seen as reflecting business growth of Taiwan firms and a good economic outlook," state radio quoted Chiang Pin-kung, chairman of cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development, as saying.
Chiang cautioned, however, that some stocks may have risen due to speculative bidding so that the level of the index could not necessarily be seen as an explicit indicator of economic health.
"Speculative actions in the stock market are inevitable and it is therefore hard to say the growth of the index truly represents the economic strength of Taiwan," Chiang said.
Chiang's comment came hours after the red-hot Taiwan share index surged past 10,000 to close at 10,066.35 -- its highest level since early 1990.

Chiang sought to draw a contrast between Taiwan's current economy and stock surge, and the last big stock market rise of 1990, when the index peaked at a frothy 12,495, only to freefall 80 percent over the next eight months.
Analysts said Chiang's comments appeared intended as a mild caution to stock-crazed investors that they should not be lulled into thinking that Taiwan's economy is invincible.

Chiang said that while some current conditions echo those in 1990, including a high trade surplus, an abundant money supply and relatively stable political conditions, today's economy is far more sophisticated and diversified than that of 1990.

Chiang said investors today face a broad array of investment channels, unlike in 1990 when the stock market was virtually the only game in town for individual investors, a situation that led extreme flows of capital into stocks.
"This resulted in the sharp stock market rally and when the heat wave passed, the market crashed," Chiang said.
